::: {.why}
Before any language model, the simplest text features on filings have documented predictive content, and they are the baseline any expensive method has to beat.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Build two simple text features from filings and evaluate them through the standard signal pipeline.
- Say why a dictionary built for general English gives the wrong sign on financial text.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Build two features: the year-over-year change in filing length, and the fraction of words in a negative-sentiment list. Use scikit-learn's CountVectorizer with a finance-specific word list rather than a general one, and note that words like liability and cost are negative in general English and neutral in a balance sheet, which is why the general lists fail here.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Evaluate both through the standard pipeline and generate their pages. Then report the coverage and the lag: a filing is text you can read the moment it appears, so the timing convention here is a filing timestamp rather than a session date, which your store already supports.
:::
:::

- [SEC EDGAR full-text search](https://www.sec.gov/edgar/search/) [data]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Two text-derived signals evaluated through the standard pipeline, with filing-timestamp lag handling and coverage reported.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Why does a general-purpose sentiment dictionary give the wrong answer on a 10-K, and what do you use instead?
:::
